definition: A named, common student misconception: a vertical bounce's up-down position curve happens to visually resemble the ball's actual up-and-down trajectory in the viewport, which misleads new animators into expecting a curve's 2D SHAPE (as drawn on the graph) to generally resemble the motion's own visible shape — in general (any rotation, any combined multi-axis motion, most real character work) the two have NO visual resemblance to each other at all, and the graph must be read as an abstract slope/value-over-time diagram, never as a literal picture of the motion.
purpose: Prevent a specific, named, recurring point of confusion by explicitly flagging the one deceptively-matching case (vertical translation) as the exception rather than the rule, before it teaches the wrong intuition.
visible_effect: A vertical bounce's translate-Y curve happens to look like a series of arcs resembling the ball's own path; a rotation curve for the same ball flipping over, by contrast, is just a rising or falling line with no visual resemblance whatsoever to "a ball flipping" as seen in the viewport.
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: Not applicable — an authoring-literacy point about how to correctly interpret a graph editor, not a viewer-facing effect.
use_cases: any curve on a rotation channel, a scale channel, or any translation axis not aligned with the obvious visual direction of motion — none of these should be expected to visually resemble the corresponding on-screen motion
teaching or learning the graph editor for the first time, specifically to avoid over-generalizing from the one coincidentally-matching example (a simple vertical bounce) most tutorials lead with
non_use_cases: the specific, narrow case of a straightforward vertical bounce, where the curve's shape and the ball's visible trajectory genuinely do resemble each other — explicitly named as the exception, not grounds for a general rule
interactions: curve_slope_as_velocity_dictionary (this same video) — this entry is the necessary caveat to that one: the slope-as-velocity dictionary is universally true and must be applied to the curve as an abstract diagram, specifically BECAUSE the curve's overall shape cannot be trusted to resemble the motion itself
cadence_representation: Not a capability gap — a purely conceptual/pedagogical clarification about how a human should INTERPRET a curve, with no corresponding Cadence tool behavior to check or measure. Worth recording anyway because it is exactly the kind of misconception a future explanatory or teaching-oriented feature (or an AI assistant narrating a curve to a user) could just as easily reproduce if it described a rotation curve's shape as if it visually mapped onto the resulting motion.
detection_and_measurement_methods: not applicable — a human-interpretation caveat, not a measurable project property.
failure_modes: expecting a rotation or multi-axis curve's 2D shape to visually resemble the resulting motion, then being confused when it does not
over-generalizing from a single vertical-bounce example (the most common first graph-editor lesson) to assume all curves work that way
examples: "in this very particular case when you're doing a ball bounce and you're doing the up-and-down of the ball the actual motion of the ball and the way the curve looks happen to look and act the same, that's not a normal thing... don't expect that your rotations and all of your translations are going to look the way they look in the viewport... and exactly match the curve of a line... this is something animation students struggle a little bit with" (video @ 02:17–02:51)
evidence_status: video: https://youtu.be/RQ31vjgJM2c @ 02:17–02:51 — Sir Wade Neistadt names this exact misconception and its one deceptive exception explicitly, unprompted, before teaching the graph editor further; experimental until validated
